entry.title: SAP Joule Work mobile app version 3.2 brings exciting new features
entry.content:
Let's have a look at the new features that got released for both experiences, the Joule Work experience, as well as the SAP Build Work Zone experience – formally called SAP Mobile Start.

Let´s start with the features that are valid for both experiences.

With the latest release, Joule conversations are now shared between mobile and web, meaning you can start a conversation on mobile and then continue it on your laptop or desktop computer. Certainly, also expired conversations will be available on mobile and web.

The new Profile and Settings entry “Conversations” allows you to see your user profile data and to enable/ disable the Joule memory feature right in the mobile app. When turned on, Joule remembers your preferences, workflows, and chat goals to keep responses relevant and fast. Memories are usually kept for 12 months, but you can revoke consent anytime by deactivating its toggle, then the memories are deleted immediately. You can always see the stored data under “Saved Memories”.

 Screenshot: New setting entry for conversations: Memory

You can now engage in natural voice conversations with Joule Work in the mobile app. With the latest release, you can speak directly to Joule and receive spoken responses, eliminating the need to look at your device screen. This hands-free experience is particularly useful when you are on the go or need to work without interacting with your device. The new Apple CarPlay integration also enables you to communicate with Joule while driving—for example, to prepare for your next customer meeting. 

 Screenshot: Joule Work in Apple Carplay

Since the last release, we allow you to customize the Support Section on the "Profile and Settings" screen. This allows you to add additional information for your users, in case they have any support needs. Now, administrators can additionally add free text to this section. Once configured, the info is displayed on the Profile and Settings screen as well as during the onboarding process. The feature can be added and configured via SAP Mobile Services or via Mobile Device Management (MDM) . Please also check our SAP Help documentation for details.

Finally, administrators can select a dedicated browser via MDM for the onboarding process. This feature can be used to define the browser the Joule Work mobile app uses for the initial onboarding authentication and possible re-authentication and allows you to enforce a specific browser policy across your managed device fleet. The setting does not affect the general in-app browsing behavior. 
We also have added Thai to the list of supported languages for SAP Joule mobile app.

Next, let´s have a look at the new feature for only Joule Work experience.

You can now view insights on your spaces and cards. Just tap on the overflow menu (three dots) of a space and select “Open Insights”. Then the insights overlay appears and provides info such as which steps got executed and which sources got leveraged to create the space.

Screenshot: Insights on Spaces

Finally, what is new for SAP Build Work Zone experience?

With the last release we had introduced workspaces for SAP Build Work Zone, advanced edition. Since then, you can easily access your workspaces when being away from your desk with the Joule Work mobile app. Now, you can also add your favorite workspaces to the Start screen, with your changes synced automatically across mobile and web. To add a workspace to the Start screen, just do a long tap on a workspace tile and add it – the same way you know from adding app favorites.  

I hope you will enjoy these features in the Joule Work mobile app.

Visit SAP Mobile Experience Community Page and click “follow” to get the latest development and innovation of our solutions. We look forward to hearing about your experience with setting up the solution in your landscape; please do share your thoughts and comments below. Enter here for additional questions regarding SAP Mobile Experience Applications.

Want to be notified? Check your profile settings to ensure you have your settings activated.

entry.title: SAP Developer tools are available on Open VSX Registry
entry.content:
SAP Developer Tools Are Now on Open VSX Registry!

 

Why That Matters

Developers don’t all work in the same editor. Some live in Visual Studio Code or VS Code. Some use Eclipse Theia-based environments in the cloud. And a growing number run AI-native editors where VS Code compatibility is the baseline — but the Microsoft Marketplace is not.

This isn’t a niche edge case. The VS Code-compatible editor ecosystem has expanded significantly, and Microsoft’s extension marketplace is not accessible from most of them. For SAP developers working in those environments, that has historically meant missing out on the tooling they need to build SAP applications effectively.

We hope that this changes with SAP’s publication on Open VSX (open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE).

What Is Open VSX Registry?

Open VSX is a vendor-neutral extension registry operated by the Eclipse Foundation. It is the standard distribution channel for VS Code extensions in any editor that does not have direct access to the Microsoft Marketplace — which covers a wide and growing set of environments used by professional developers today.

 

Where the Microsoft Marketplace is tied to the Microsoft ecosystem, Open VSX is open infrastructure. Any VS Code-compatible editor can consume it. Any publisher can list extensions without vendor agreements. It is how the broader editor ecosystem accesses the extension tooling it needs.

SAP’s Developer Strategy: Choice Without Compromise

SAP’s position is straightforward: developers should be able to work in the environment that makes them most productive. The SAP tooling needed to build cloud applications, Fiori UIs, and mobile solutions should follow them there — not require them to switch editors.

 

Publishing on Open VSX is how SAP delivers on that. It ensures that SAP’s developer extensions are available wherever VS Code-compatible editors are used, without requiring developers to compromise on their setup.

This is the direct continuation of the work announced in this VS Code extensions blog.

What’s Published Under the SAPSE Namespace

The following eight extensions are available today at open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE:

SAP CDS Language Support

Language support for SAP Core Data Services delivers syntax highlighting, Language Server Protocol integration, real-time diagnostics, and formatting for .cds files. The foundational extension for SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) development — if you’re building CAP services, this is where you start.

Core Data Services Graphical Modeler

CDS Graphical Modeler allows the developer to model CDS files in SAP Cloud Application Programming model development projects and enables increased productivity in designing CDS model via the graphical editor. Both CAP (.cds) and ABAP CDS (.csn) files can be edited.

SAP Fiori Tools — Extension Pack

A bundled pack that installs the full SAP Fiori development toolchain in one step. The recommended starting point for any Fiori Elements or SAPUI5 project.

SAP Fiori Tools — Application Modeler

A visual representation of a Fiori application’s page structure, navigation targets, and service entities. The Page Map view lets you add navigation, manage pages, and modify application structure directly — no manual configuration file editing required.

SAP Fiori Tools — XML Annotation Language Server

Authoring support for OData annotations — the metadata layer that drives how Fiori Elements applications render and behave. Provides code completion, micro-snippets, i18n support, and real-time diagnostics as you write annotation files.

SAP Fiori Tools — Service Modeler

A combined view of an OData service and its associated annotations helping to understand a service’s structure and annotation coverage without parsing raw metadata — particularly when connecting Fiori applications to SAP backend systems.

SAP Fiori Tools — Guided Development

In-editor access to how-to guides and step-by-step tutorials for implementing Fiori Elements features. Contextual guidance surfaces during development, so the relevant SAP documentation is available without leaving the editor.

Mobile Development Kit Editor

Visual development tools for the mobile development kit, SAP's platform for building enterprise-grade cross-platform mobile applications with offline capabilities, OData backend synchronization, and deployment across iOS and Android. The end-to-end development capabilities includes visual editing, debugging support, and code snippets, enabling developers to build, debug, and maintain mobile applications directly within the IDE.

Getting Started

If you’re working in a Visual Studio Code-compatible editor, search for SAPSE in your extension marketplace — or navigate directly to open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE. 

While Visual Studio Code users can continue using the Microsoft Marketplace/SAP SE as before. Open VSX serves developers who work in other growing ecosystem of editors built on VS Code’s foundations.

The extensions are the same. The tooling is the same. The only difference is that more developers can now use it — in the editor they choose.

Follow SAP Application Development on the SAP Community for updates on developer tooling, CAP, Fiori development, and mobile.

entry.title: MDK for Windows 4.1 – Using the Calendar Control in SSAM for Windows
entry.content:
Overview

With the upcoming MDK for Windows 4.1, we introduced several new capabilities that bring the Windows client closer to the experience available on other MDK platforms (MDK for Windows 4.1 new features). One of these additions is the new Calendar Control, which enables customers to build calendar-based user experiences in their Windows applications.

MDK for Windows 4.1 was designed as an MDK-only release, without a corresponding SAP Service and Asset Manager (SSAM) for Windows 4.1 release. Customers using SSAM for Windows 4.0 can nevertheless take advantage of the new MDK capabilities when building a custom client. The prerequisite is an existing SSAM for Windows 4.0 custom build, where the MDK for Windows dependency is upgraded from version 4.0 to 4.1 (Upgrading from MDK for Windows 4.0 to 4.1).

Once the custom client is built with MDK for Windows 4.1, the Calendar Control becomes available for use. Since the control is provided by the MDK SDK and is not part of the standard SSAM for Windows 4.0 application, it needs to be integrated into the customer's custom application.

The Calendar Control offers a broad set of capabilities for building calendar-based experiences in MDK applications. For a complete overview of the available features, properties, and APIs, see the Calendar Control documentation and API reference. In this blog post, we focus on a representative set of features that are commonly used in real-world scenarios: date selection, date range selection, event indicators, event generation, and interaction through the ICalendarProxy. Together, these examples provide a practical introduction to integrating the Calendar Control into a custom SSAM for Windows 4.0 client using MDK for Windows 4.1.

1. Add a Week-Mode Calendar

Drop a Section.Type.Calendar into a SectionedTable. Minimal metadata:

{
    "CalendarType": "Week",
    "IsPersistentSelection": true,
    "OnSelectedDateChange": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateSelected.js",
    "SelectedDate": "2024-06-11T00:00:00",
    "_Name": "CalendarSection",
    "_Type": "Section.Type.Calendar"
}

(Note that setting the SelectedDate is for our convenience, because our example data has a DueDate on that week. The Calendar opens with today selected by default if this field is omitted.)

Just below the calendar, we'll add an example ObjectTable so that we have something to do with the selected dates (we're going to filter an entity set based on the selected date).

{
    "_Type": "Section.Type.ObjectTable",
    "_Name": "CalendarFilteredServiceOrderDataTable",
    "Header": {
        "UseTopPadding": true,
        "Caption": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateFilteredSOHeaderCaption.js"
    },
    "EmptySection": {
        "Caption": "nothing to see here"
    },
    "MaxItemCount": 4,
    "ObjectCell": {
        "Title": "{Description}",
        "Subhead": "{ObjectID}",
        "Footnote": "{DueBy}"
    },
    "Target": {
        "EntitySet": "S4ServiceOrders",
        "QueryOptions": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateFilteredSOQuery.js",
        "Service": "/SAPAssetManager/Services/AssetManager.service"
    }
},

With these added, we have the resulting sections on our overview page:

2. Handle Date Selection with ICalendarProxy

The OnSelectedDateChange handler receives an ICalendarProxy (extends ISectionProxy). Calendar-specific methods:

export default function DateSelected(/** @type {ICalendarProxy} */ cp) {
    const calendarType = cp.getCalendarType();  // 'Week'
    const selectedDate = String(cp.getSelectedDate());  // e.g.: 'Tue Jun 11 2024 00:00:00 GMT+0200'
}

If we want to trigger something when the selection changes, this is the place to do so. With the Target's DataQuery set up to fetch the selected date from the calendar, we can just force a redraw on our example ObjectTable (a more elegant solution would be to use the setTargetSpecifier or the setFilters methods of the ObjectTableProxy, because most of the time fully decorated ObjectTables are extracted out to reusable fragments used on several pages and we don't want to couple them with a page specific control like this calendar. Keep in mind, in our example we still leave the initial values bound to calendar in the rules for better tracability, these could go into an OnLoaded rule if we wanted true decoupling. See later code snippets below for a different DateSelected implementation):

export default function DateSelected(/** @type {ICalendarProxy} */ cp) {
    const dataTable = cp.getPageProxy().getControls().find(i => i.getType() === 'Control.Type.SectionedTable').getSection('CalendarFilteredServiceOrderDataTable');
    dataTable.redraw();
}

This is the query set up for the ServiceOrders:

export default function DateFilteredSOQuery(/** @type {ISectionedTableProxy} */ context) {
    /** @type {ICalendarProxy} */ 
    const calendarSection = context.getPageProxy().getControls()?.find(i => i.getType() === 'Control.Type.SectionedTable')?.getSection('CalendarSection');
    const selectedDate = calendarSection?.getSelectedDate() ?? new Date(2024, 6, 11);  // e.g.: Date('Fri Sep 25 2026 00:00:00 GMT+0200')
    const fromDate = new ODataDate(selectedDate);
    const toDate = new ODataDate((new Date(selectedDate)).setDate(selectedDate.getDate() + 1));
    return `$filter=(DueBy ge ${fromDate.queryString(context, 'date')} and DueBy lt ${toDate.queryString(context, 'date')})`;
}​

We fetch our Calendar control from the sectiontable by name, then fetch the selected date. In case we cannot find the control, we fall back to the set default value (the same '24 June 11 we set in the page metadata file, out of convenience). The naive implementation would then check for field equality, but we have the a priori knowledge from the odata CSDL schema (or the MAIF configpanel omdo configuration), that the DueBy property of the S4ServiceOrder entity is of type Edm.DateTime. This means that the DueBy can carry time data as well, which our picked date from the calendar does not (it is midnight based), so we have to apply an interval filter: pickedDate <= DueBy < pickedDate + 1 day. In practice a filter query looks something like so: 

"$filter=(DueBy ge datetime'2024-06-11T00:00:00' and DueBy lt datetime'2024-06-12T00:00:00'"​

At this point we could get into the server time offset adjustments (local timezone vs server timezone), but in this example we're omitting that for brevity.
For the Header Caption we just reused the same filter with a count invokation:

import DateFilteredSOQuery from "./DateFilteredSOQuery";

export default function DateFilteredSOHeaderCaption(/** @type {ISectionHeaderProxy} */ context) {
    return Promise.all([
        context.count('/SAPAssetManager/Services/AssetManager.service', 'S4ServiceOrders', DateFilteredSOQuery(context)),
        context.count('/SAPAssetManager/Services/AssetManager.service', 'S4ServiceOrders')
    ]).then(([filteredCount, totalCount]) => `Filtered ServiceOrders (${filteredCount} of ${totalCount})`);
}

Now if we pick a day in the calendar where there is a S4ServiceOrder with a DueBy datetime, we should be seeing it reflected in our example section:

3. Add Calendar Indicators

With indicators we can highlight events in the calendar, making them visible for the operators. Our example will highlight the S4ServiceOrders based on their status. In order to achieve this we need to add a couple of new field to our calendar metadata (along with the corresponding rules. Notice the Indicators, Targets and Event properties):

{
    ...
    "SelectedDate": "2024-06-11T00:00:00",
    "Indicators": [
        { "_Name": "_Open", "Title": "Open", "Icon": "/SAPAssetManager/Images/trafficlight_red.light.png" },
        { "_Name": "_InProcess", "Title": "In Process", "Icon": "/SAPAssetManager/Images/trafficlight_orange.light.png" },
        { "_Name": "_Released", "Title": "Released", "Icon": "/SAPAssetManager/Images/trafficlight_green.dark.png" }
    ],
    "Targets": [
        {
            "Service": "/SAPAssetManager/Services/AssetManager.service",
            "EntitySet": "S4ServiceOrders",
            "DateProperties": ["DueBy"]
        }
    ],
    "Event": {
        "IndicatorName": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateResolveEventIndicator.js"
    },
    ...
},

It is worth noting that the Indicators property could also be moved into a separate rule file that returns the same JavaScript array. Here we show how to use events read from an odata entityset (with the Target specifier), but we could use the calendar with "static" events as well, where static means the events are fabricated either in a js rule or directly into the calendar metadata json, in that case we'd use the "Events" property instead of the "Event"+"Target" (Event and Target take prededence over Events in case all of them are present).

The related IndicatorName rule:

export default function DateResolveEventIndicator(/** @type {ICalendarProxy} */ cp) {
    const entitySets = cp?.binding?.EntitySets;
    const orders = entitySets?.S4ServiceOrders;
    if (!orders || orders.length === 0) {
        return undefined;
    }
    // First-record-wins: when multiple orders share the date, the first one's StatusDesc drives the indicator.
    const status = orders[0]?.StatusDesc;
    return {'Open': '_Open', 'In Process': '_InProcess', 'Released': '_Released'}[status];
}

The rule is run once per entityset for each day, so if there is a day with several entities for that date, this is the place to pick which indicator they all translate to (in conclusion, if there were multiple orders for the same day they all have to have the same indicator). Through our example, this means if we had e.g. 2 'Open' orders for Monday, we'd have the 'Open' indicator with the label '2' noting there are 2 events of the type. In essence this rule is the one mapping the entityTypes to their indicator types.

 

4. Switch from Week Mode to DateRange Mode

So far, the user has selected a single date. The Calendar control can also allow the user to select a range of dates by changing CalendarType from Week to DateRange. This requires three corresponding changes:

  • Replace SelectedDate with SelectedDateRange.
  • Replace OnSelectedDateChange with OnSelectedDateRangeChange.
  • Use getSelectedDateRange() instead of getSelectedDate() in the selection handler.
...
"OnSelectedDateRangeChange": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateSelected.js",
"SelectedDateRange": {
    "_Type": "Calendar.Type.DateRange",
    "StartDate": "2024-06-11T00:00:00",
    "EndDate": "2024-06-14T00:00:00"
},
"Indicators": [
...

In our first example the date filtering is set up in the query rule of the objecttable target, let's see how it would look like with setTargetSpecifier from the DateSelected rule. First we're going to fetch the selected daterange with getSelectedDateRange instead of a single day with getSelectedDate and use the start date as our lower bound and the end date + 1 day as our upper bound for filtering (start <= day < end + 1), then we'll get the existing TargetSpecifier and change the filter in it, then set it to the objecttable.

export default function DateSelected(/** @type {ICalendarProxy} */ cp) {
    /** @type {IDateRangeProxy | { startDate: Date, endDate: Date }} */
    const selectedDateRange = cp.getSelectedDateRange();

    const fromDate = new ODataDate(selectedDateRange.startDate);
    const toDate = new ODataDate((new Date(selectedDateRange.endDate)).setDate(selectedDateRange.endDate.getDate() + 1));
    const filterQuery = `$filter=(DueBy ge ${fromDate.queryString(cp, 'date')} and DueBy lt ${toDate.queryString(cp, 'date')})`;
    
    /** @type {IObjectTableProxy} */
    const dataTable = cp.getPageProxy().getControls().find(i => i.getType() === 'Control.Type.SectionedTable').getSection('CalendarFilteredServiceOrderDataTable');
    let targetSpec = dataTable.getTargetSpecifier();
    targetSpec.setQueryOptions(filterQuery);
    return Promise.all([
        dataTable.setTargetSpecifier(targetSpec, true),
        SetHeaderCaption(dataTable.getHeader(), filterQuery),
    ]);
}

For decoupling the objecttable from the calendar, we changed the way we set the header, so it is now bound to the page's clientData, with the default value of 'Filtered ServiceOrders' in case we havent set anything to the clientData property yet:

"Header": {
    "UseTopPadding": true,
    "Caption": "$(DV, '#Page:-Current/#ClientData/#Property:CalendarFilteredServiceOrderDataTableHeaderLabel', 'Filtered ServiceOrders')"
},​

We placed the caption helper functions right next to the DateSelected function:

function ObjectTableHeaderCaption(/** @type {ISectionHeaderProxy} */ hp, filterQuery) {
    return Promise.all([
        hp.count('/SAPAssetManager/Services/AssetManager.service', 'S4ServiceOrders', filterQuery),
        hp.count('/SAPAssetManager/Services/AssetManager.service', 'S4ServiceOrders')
    ]).then(([filteredCount, totalCount]) => `Filtered ServiceOrders (${filteredCount} of ${totalCount})`);
}

function SetHeaderCaption(/** @type {ISectionHeaderProxy} */ hp, filterQuery) {
    return ObjectTableHeaderCaption(hp, filterQuery)
        .then(caption => {
            hp.getPageProxy().getClientData().CalendarFilteredServiceOrderDataTableHeaderLabel = caption;
            hp.redraw();
        });
}​

We needed to tend to the header separately, because by setting the TargetSpecifier to the ObjectTable, the header itself is not redrawn.

5. Generate Events and Indicators from Rules

As we stated earlier, the events can be constructed "by hand" as well, not just fetched from an odata service. These can go directly into the page metadata, or bound via a rule which returns them in an array in the same shape. In our example, we went with the rule based option.

Notice, how the Target and Event properties are gone and we have Events instead with a rule (this could have been a hardcoded array with the events too). Unrelated to this, we also moved the Indicators to their own rule.

{
    "CalendarType": "DateRange",
    "OnSelectedDateRangeChange": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateSelected.js",
    "IsPersistentSelection": true,
    "SelectedDateRange": {
        "_Type": "Calendar.Type.DateRange",
        "StartDate": "2024-06-11T00:00:00",
        "EndDate": "2024-06-14T00:00:00"
    },
    "Indicators": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateIndicatorNames.js",
    "Events": "/SAPAssetManager/Rules/ServiceOrders/DateFixedEvents.js",
    "_Name": "CalendarSection",
    "_Type": "Section.Type.Calendar"
},

In this example, we create two Open events per day for ten days, one In Process event every second day, and one Released event every third day.

export default function DateFixedEvents(/** @type {ICalendarProxy} */ cp) {
    return [
        ...Array.from({length: 10}, (_, i) => ({ Date: `2024-06-${10 + i}T00:00:00`, IndicatorName: '_Open' })),
        ...Array.from({length: 10}, (_, i) => ({ Date: `2024-06-${10 + i}T00:00:00`, IndicatorName: '_Open' })),
        ...Array.from({length: 10}, (_, i) => ({ Date: `2024-06-${10 + i * 2}T00:00:00`, IndicatorName: '_InProcess' })),
        ...Array.from({length: 10}, (_, i) => ({ Date: `2024-06-${10 + i * 3}T00:00:00`, IndicatorName: '_Released' })),
    ];
}

The DateIndicatorNames rule has the very same name-title-icon mapping as it did when this was in the page metadata.

export default function DateIndicatorNames(/** @type {ICalendarProxy} */ cp) {
    return [
        { "_Name": "_Open", "Title": "Open", "Icon": "/SAPAssetManager/Images/trafficlight_red.light.png" },
        { "_Name": "_InProcess", "Title": "In Process", "Icon": "/SAPAssetManager/Images/trafficlight_orange.light.png" },
        { "_Name": "_Released", "Title": "Released", "Icon": "/SAPAssetManager/Images/trafficlight_green.dark.png" },
    ];
}

In this walkthrough, we explored several key capabilities of the SSAM Windows Calendar Control, including single-date and date-range selection, user interaction through ICalendarProxy, status-based indicators, ObjectTable filtering, and rule-driven event generation. These examples demonstrate common integration patterns and provide a foundation for building richer calendar-based experiences in custom MDK applications. We also used ICalendarProxy to react to user selections, filtered an ObjectTable based on those selections, displayed status-based indicators, and demonstrated how calendar events and indicators can be generated dynamically from rules.
